traveler: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq (Abd Allah ibn Abi Quhafa)
title: The Second of the Two: from the Camel Pens of Mecca to the Chamber Beside the Prophet
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Cloth Merchant of Banu Taym

stops.name: Mecca, the house of Abu Quhafa: a son of Banu Taym
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the year is given as c. 573 or 574 and no source attests a month or a day
stops.campa: In a house of the Banu Taym quarter, a few streets from the Kaaba, a son is born to Abu Quhafa and Umm al-Khayr. They name him Abd Allah. Mecca will know him better by a nickname earned among the camel pens: Abu Bakr, father of the young camel. He grows into a cloth merchant with a memory for lineages, the man Quraysh consult when they want to know whose grandfather married whose, and the man they trust with a deposit. Neither the year nor the house is fixed by any document; the city keeps him without an address.
suggested_refs: The Banu Taym quarter of pre-Islamic Mecca; the pin is approximate, near the Haram, where Quraysh households clustered

stops.name: Busra, the caravan road into Syria
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the sources attest the pattern of his trade, not any single journey or year
stops.campa: Long before there is anything to believe, the roads carry him north. Quraysh caravans run cloth and hides and incense up the Hijaz to Busra in the Byzantine province of Syria, and Abu Bakr rides with them, as Muhammad ibn Abd Allah rides with them, both of them merchants of the same city on the same road. He learns the price of goods in four markets and the manners of Christian Syria. This route is the whole of his known world for thirty years, and it is the road his armies will take at the end of his life.
suggested_refs: The Quraysh caravan route from Mecca to Busra, the winter and summer journeys of Surah Quraysh
sources: general Quraysh caravan-trade tradition, reported in Wikipedia, 'Abu Bakr'

stops.name: Mecca, the house of Muhammad: the assent without argument
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the order of the earliest converts is disputed between Sunni and Shia tradition and Ibn Kathir declines to rank them at all
stops.campa: Muhammad tells him what came to him on Hira, and Abu Bakr believes without argument. Sunni tradition counts him the first free adult man to enter Islam; Shia tradition gives that place to Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Ibn Kathir declines to rank the early converts at all, sorting them by household instead. What no source disputes is what follows him in. Uthman ibn Affan, Talha ibn Ubayd Allah, al-Zubayr and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas come through his advocacy. He is the first man in Mecca whose word is worth something to the new faith.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json, 'Mecca, the first believers'
sources: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (trans. Guillaume)

stops.name: Mecca, the Kaaba: beaten before the sanctuary
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: Muhammad preaches openly for the first time in the precinct of the Kaaba, and Abu Bakr stands and speaks after him. Quraysh youths set on him there, in front of the sanctuary his own clan helps to guard, and beat him until he is carried off senseless. When he comes to, the first thing he asks is whether Muhammad is alive. His mother Umm al-Khayr, watching her son bleed for it, becomes a Muslim herself. The precinct is the same one his caravans have circled since he was a boy, and the ground is the ground he will ride back into at sixty.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba pin, 21.4225 / 39.8262, shared exactly with muhammad.journey.json and aishah.journey.json

stops.name: Mecca, the Dar al-Arqam on the slope of al-Safa
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the sources place the meetings here without dating their beginning or end
stops.campa: The believers meet in secret at the house of al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam on the slope of al-Safa, close enough to the Kaaba to hear the pilgrims and screened enough to teach in. Abu Bakr comes and brings others: the wealthy, the well-connected, men whose conversion costs Quraysh something real. He is forty years old, established, and spending his standing as freely as his money. Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabari both put the gatherings in this house, and neither of them says on what day it stopped being safe.
suggested_refs: The Dar al-Arqam near al-Safa, first house of instruction in Islam

stops.name: Mecca, the sand outside the houses: Bilal bought free
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: Umayya ibn Khalaf takes his slave Bilal ibn Rabah out onto the sand beyond the houses, lays him on his back under the noon sun and sets a rock on his chest to make him renounce the one God. Bilal says one word, ahad. Abu Bakr buys him and frees him, and buys and frees six others held the same way, and the manumissions eat into a merchant's fortune that will never be rebuilt. Muhammad's own journey records this hour from the other side. The tortured slave becomes the voice that will call Medina to prayer.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json, 'Bilal on the burning sands'; the torture is placed by the sources in open desert outside Mecca, not in a marketplace

segments.name: The Boycott and the Night Journey

stops.name: Bark al-Ghimad, the halt on the Yemen road
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the boycott years are dated only by their span, c. 616 to 619
stops.campa: Quraysh shut the Banu Hashim and their protectors into the ravine and cut off marriage and trade with them. Abu Bakr, his fortune worn down by the manumissions and by the boycott, sets out south for Abyssinia along the Yemen road and gets as far as a halt the sources call Bark al-Ghimad. There Ibn al-Dughunna of the Qara meets him, refuses to let a man of his kind leave Arabia, and takes him back to Mecca under personal protection. The protection lasts exactly as long as he prays quietly enough for his neighbours not to hear.
suggested_refs: Bark al-Ghimad is unlocated in any reachable source; the pin is an approximation of the Yemen road south of Mecca and should not be read as a site

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Noble Rock: the name as-Siddiq
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the derivation of the epithet from this answer is tradition and muhammad.journey.json narrates the ascent without stating the naming episode
stops.campa: Muhammad tells Mecca he has been carried in a night to the farthest mosque and up through the heavens, and Quraysh bring it to Abu Bakr as a scandal they expect him to disown. He answers that if Muhammad said it then it is true, and that he believes him about far stranger things than this, meaning revelation itself. From that answer the tradition dates his name: as-Siddiq, the one who confirms the truth. The rock he has never seen and will never see stands twelve hundred kilometres north, in a city he does not enter in his lifetime.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json, the Isra and Mi'raj stop at the Temple Mount

stops.name: Mecca, the house of Abu Bakr: Aishah betrothed
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: In the house of Abu Bakr in the Banu Taym quarter, the betrothal of his daughter Aishah to Muhammad is settled. Aishah's own journey opens in these rooms: fourth child of the house, born about four years into Islam, and the sign Muhammad reports is a form wrapped in silk that an angel showed him. Two families already bound by belief and by the caravan roads become one household in law. Abu Bakr is father-in-law to the Prophet from this year, and will be his successor twelve years later.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from aishah.journey.json, the betrothal in the house of Abu Bakr

stops.name: Mecca, the night the assassins ring the house
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the date is the one carried by muhammad.journey.json and is itself a tradition
stops.campa: Quraysh agree that one man from each clan will strike together, so that no single clan can be held to account for the blood. On the night they come, Muhammad leaves Ali in his bed and walks to the house of Abu Bakr. Abu Bakr has kept two riding camels fed and ready for months against exactly this hour, and weeps when he is told that he is to be the companion. They go out through the back of the house and turn south, away from Medina, because Medina is north and every tracker in Mecca knows it.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json, the Hijra plot

stops.name: Cave of Thawr, three nights in the rock
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: They climb Jabal Thawr in the dark and lie up three nights in a cleft near the summit while Quraysh trackers work the slope below, near enough that Abu Bakr can see their feet from inside. His daughter Asma carries food up after dark and ties the sack with half her torn waist-belt, which earns her the name Dhat al-Nitaqayn. His son Abd Allah sleeps in Mecca and brings the night's talk at dawn. Tradition sets a spider's web and a dove's nest across the mouth. The Quran will call him the second of the two.
stops.quote: If one of them (pagans) should lift up his foot, he will see us.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr to Muhammad in the cave, Sahih al-Bukhari 4663, Book of Tafsir on Qur'an 9:40, narrated by Abu Bakr; Muhammad's answer in the same narration is 'What do you think of two, the third of whom is Allah?'
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json; the geography of the research pool placed the cave 5 km away at 21.3859 / 39.8567, and the canonical atlas pin is used instead

stops.name: Qudayd, the tent of Umm Ma'bad
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the episode belongs to the later Hijra-route literature rather than to the earliest hadith
stops.campa: The guide takes them down onto the coast road to shake off pursuit, and at Qudayd they stop at the tent of Umm Ma'bad al-Khuza'iyya, who has nothing to give travellers: her herd is out at pasture and the one goat left behind is barren with hunger. The tradition says the goat gives milk at Muhammad's touch, enough for the whole party and a bowl left standing. Abu Bakr is at his side through the encounter. Her husband, coming home to a full bowl in a starving season, knows who has passed without being told.
suggested_refs: The Hijra route by the coast at Qudayd, and the hadith of Umm Ma'bad
sources: later Hijra-route traditions, reported in Wikipedia, 'Abu Bakr'

stops.name: Quba, the town comes out to the road
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: Twelve days out of Mecca they come to Quba on the edge of Yathrib, and the town comes out to meet them. The Ansar have been watching the road for days, and the tradition says they take Abu Bakr for the Prophet at first because he is the older-looking of the two, until he stands and shades Muhammad with his cloak and the crowd sorts them out. The first mosque of Islam is laid out here before either man enters the town proper. Abu Bakr has left a city, a trade and a fortune, and arrives with a companion.
suggested_refs: Masjid Quba, the first mosque, raised before the entry into Yathrib

stops.name: Medina, the household reassembled by the mosque
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; the month follows aishah.journey.json
stops.campa: Abu Bakr's household is brought up from Mecca and reassembled beside the mosque Muhammad raises in Yathrib, which is now Madinat al-Nabi. Aishah's journey rejoins his here: the daughter, the wife, the small rooms along the eastern wall. He goes down with the oasis fever in the first months, as most of the Meccans do, and recovers. For the next twelve years this mosque is the fixed point of his life, and he is never more than a courtyard away from the man he walked out of Mecca beside.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from aishah.journey.json, the Medina arrival

stops.name: Badr, the wells and the shelter on the ridge
stops.date_confidence: attested, 13 March 624 = 17 Ramadan AH 2; the sources conflict on whether Abu Bakr fought in the line or guarded the Prophet's shelter
stops.campa: Three hundred and some men meet a Quraysh army three times their number at the wells of Badr and break it. Abu Bakr is at the shelter built for the Prophet on the ridge, and the accounts divide over what that means: some make him a guard at the door of it, others put him in the fighting line, and one tradition attributed to Ali presents the guard post as the braver of the two. His son Abd al-Rahman is in the ranks opposite, still a Meccan. The Quraysh dead include men he has bought and sold with for thirty years.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Badr; the pin sits on the modern town, about 6 km from the traditional site

stops.name: Uhud, the line breaks and closes
stops.date_confidence: attested, 7 Shawwal AH 3
stops.campa: The archers leave the hill, Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry comes round behind them, and the Muslim line breaks with a cry going up that Muhammad is dead. Abu Bakr is one of the handful who cut back through to him, find him alive with his face laid open, and get him up the slope of Uhud out of reach. Abu Bakr takes wounds of his own in the press around the Prophet. Seventy Muslims are left on the field, Hamza among them. Khalid, who wins the day for Mecca here, will be Abu Bakr's own general in nine years.
suggested_refs: The slope of Mount Uhud and the graves of the martyrs of Uhud

stops.name: Medina, the Trench: a sector held for a month
stops.date_confidence: traditional, Shawwal AH 5; the sources give the month and not the day
stops.campa: Ten thousand men come up from Mecca and the tribes to finish Medina, and the city digs. On Salman al-Farisi's advice a trench is cut across the open northern approach, and Abu Bakr digs with the rest and then holds a sector of the line through a month of cold and skirmishing. The confederates never cross it. Wind, hunger and their own quarrels break the siege instead, and the army that came to end Islam goes home without a battle. A mosque is built afterwards on the ground he held, which is how Medina records who stood where.
suggested_refs: The Masjid Abu Bakr among the Seven Mosques at the trench line, built on the sector he held

stops.name: Al-Hudaybiyya, the treaty that looks like a defeat
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month and year, Dhu al-Qa'da AH 6
stops.campa: The pilgrims put on ihram at Dhul Hulayfah and ride for Mecca unarmed, and Quraysh stop them at the wells of al-Hudaybiyya. The treaty Muhammad signs reads to the army like a surrender: ten years of truce, no pilgrimage this year, converts fleeing Mecca to be handed back. Umar takes his objection to the Prophet and then to Abu Bakr, who tells him to hold to the man's stirrup and not let go. Abu Bakr does not need the terms explained to him twice, and the Quran will call the day a clear victory.
suggested_refs: Dhul Hulayfah, the miqat where the pilgrims entered ihram, and the wells of al-Hudaybiyya

stops.name: Khaybar, the forts and a contested banner
stops.date_confidence: attested as to season, Muharram AH 7, May or June 628
stops.campa: The oasis of Khaybar holds out fort by fort behind basalt walls, and the siege runs for weeks. One tradition, carried hardest by the partisans of Ali, sends Abu Bakr against the fortress of al-Qamus with the banner and has him come back without taking it, and Umar after him, before the banner passes to Ali and the gate falls. The story is old and it is told for a purpose, attached to the hadith of the banner given to a man who loves God. What is not in dispute is that Abu Bakr is at Khaybar and that Khaybar falls.
suggested_refs: The basalt forts of the Khaybar oasis, and the partisan literature attached to al-Qamus

stops.name: Mecca, the Kaaba: the city taken without a battle
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month, 10 Ramadan AH 8
stops.campa: Ten thousand come down on Mecca and the city opens without a battle. Abu Bakr rides in at fifty-seven, past the pens where he earned his nickname, past the ground where he was beaten senseless for speaking, past the sand where he bought Bilal, who now climbs onto the roof of the Kaaba to give the call. The three hundred and sixty idols around the House are pulled down and broken. He leads his blind father Abu Quhafa out to give allegiance, and Muhammad tells him he should have left the old man at home and come to him instead.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba pin, shared exactly with muhammad.journey.json and abdelkader.journey.json

stops.name: Ta'if, the siege lifted on his advice
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month, February 630, AH 8; the siege ran about half a month
stops.campa: Hunayn nearly undoes the whole conquest: the army is ambushed in the defile, the new Meccan converts run, and about nine men hold the ground around Muhammad. Abu Bakr is one of the nine. The survivors of Hawazin shut themselves into Ta'if behind walls the Muslims have no engines to break, and after roughly a fortnight of it Abu Bakr is the one who advises lifting the siege. The advice is taken and the army marches away. Ta'if sends its submission a year later, unbesieged, and the Banu Thaqif come in of their own accord.
suggested_refs: The walls of Ta'if; no coordinates for the defile of Hunayn were verified, so that engagement is narrated here rather than pinned

stops.name: Tabuk, everything he owns given away
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month, Rajab AH 9
stops.campa: A rumour of Byzantine mobilisation on the Syrian frontier pulls the army north in the worst of the heat, on the march the sources remember as the hard one. Abu Bakr brings his entire property to the collection, every dirham of it. Asked what he has left for his family, he answers that he has left them God and His Messenger, and Umar, who has given half of his, stops competing on the spot. The army sits at Tabuk for twenty days, finds no Byzantine force in front of it, and turns for home along the road he first rode as a merchant.
suggested_refs: The camp at Tabuk on the Syrian frontier; the answer to Muhammad is reported speech in Abu Dawud and al-Tabari and was not verified verbatim, so it is narrated rather than quoted

stops.name: Mina, amir al-hajj: the pilgrimage commanded
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month, Dhu al-Hijja AH 9
stops.campa: Muhammad appoints him amir al-hajj, commander of the pilgrimage, and Abu Bakr leads some three hundred pilgrims down to Mecca, the first hajj administered by Muslims since the conquest. At Mina, Ali overtakes the caravan carrying the opening verses of Surah at-Tawbah and reads them to the assembled tribes: after this year no idolater performs the pilgrimage and no one circles the House naked. Abu Bakr commands the rite and Ali proclaims the text, and both facts will be cited later by people arguing about succession.
suggested_refs: The valley of Mina; the proclamation of Surah at-Tawbah at the pilgrimage of AH 9

stops.name: Mount Arafat, the Farewell Sermon
stops.date_confidence: attested, 9 Dhu al-Hijja AH 10
stops.campa: On the ninth of Dhu al-Hijja the whole community stands on the plain below the mount of Arafat, and Muhammad speaks from the back of a camel about blood debts cancelled, usury cancelled, the rights of women, and an Arab holding no precedence over a non-Arab. Abu Bakr is somewhere in that crowd. It is the last time the community will be assembled in one place with the Prophet standing in front of it. Some who are there hear it as a farewell before anyone in Medina has said the word out loud.
suggested_refs: The plain of Arafat and the Jabal al-Rahma, station of the Farewell Pilgrimage

stops.name: Medina, the mosque: leading the prayer in the Prophet's illness
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact and the month; that the instruction was a succession signal is a later Sunni reading
stops.campa: The fever takes hold in Aishah's room and Muhammad can no longer walk out to the prayer. He orders Abu Bakr to lead it. Aishah asks twice for somebody else, saying that her father is a soft-hearted man who will never get through the recitation for weeping, and is told twice to let Abu Bakr lead. He leads through the last days of the illness, with the sick man sometimes carried out to pray behind him. Whether this was an instruction about prayer or an instruction about succession is the question the next fourteen centuries divide over.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json and aishah.journey.json, the Medina mosque and the rooms along its eastern wall

stops.name: Medina, the Sacred Chamber: the death of Muhammad
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On a Monday in June, in the chamber against the east wall of the mosque, Muhammad dies leaning on Aishah. Umar stands in the courtyard with his sword and says he will cut the legs off any man who claims the Prophet is dead. Abu Bakr rides in from al-Sunh, goes past him into the room, uncovers the face, kisses it and covers it again, then comes out and speaks. Aishah is eighteen, and in her own journey she watches from these rooms as the faith she was born inside changes hands.
stops.quote: If anyone worships Muhammad, Muhammad is dead. If anyone worships God, God is alive, immortal.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr to the community at Muhammad's death, Medina, 8 June 632, in Wikipedia's rendering; muhammad.journey.json carries a different English of the same address from Sahih al-Bukhari, 'whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad is dead; whoever worships God, God is living', quoting Qur'an 3:144. Two translation traditions, one Arabic original.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json and aishah.journey.json, al-Hujra al-Sharifa

stops.name: Saqifah of Banu Sa'ida, the roofed courtyard
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the day; the exact site of the Saqifah within Medina is not archaeologically fixed and the pin is approximate
stops.campa: While the body lies unwashed, the Ansar gather under the roofed courtyard of the Banu Sa'ida to choose a leader from among themselves. Abu Bakr, Umar and Abu Ubayda walk in uninvited. Abu Bakr argues that the Arabs will follow no house but Quraysh, and offers the other two men in his own place; Umar takes his hand and swears to him instead, and the room follows. Habab ibn al-Mundhir proposes one leader from each side and is refused. Umar and Sa'd ibn Ubada come to blows on the floor.
suggested_refs: The Saqifah of the Banu Sa'ida; Umar is later reported calling the proceedings a falta, a precipitate affair, while upholding the outcome

stops.name: Medina, the mosque: the general pledge
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the day after the Saqifah; aishah.journey.json dates the accession stop to July, which is the same event on a looser calendar
stops.campa: The next morning the community at large gives the oath in the mosque, and Abu Bakr, at fifty-nine, becomes the first of the four whom Sunni Islam will call the Rightly Guided. Ali and a group with him hold back for about six months before acknowledging him; Shia Islam holds that the succession was settled at Ghadir Khumm and taken here. In Aishah's journey the same morning reads from inside: not yet twenty, she watches the office pass out of her husband's hands and into her father's, in the same three rooms.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from aishah.journey.json, the accession stop

stops.name: Al-Jurf, the army of Usama sent out
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the interval, two days after Muhammad's death; the camp coordinates are approximate, al-Jurf lying a few kilometres north of Medina
stops.campa: Two days after the death he sends out Usama ibn Zayd's army for the Syrian frontier, the expedition Muhammad ordered and the whole council begs him to cancel with the peninsula in revolt behind it. He refuses to unbind what the Prophet bound, walks on foot beside the mounted boy commander who a month ago commanded him as a private soldier, and then stands up among the people and tells them plainly what he is and is not. Al-Tabari puts the speech here, at the camp of al-Jurf, and not at the pledge in the mosque.
stops.quote: Oh people, I am like you. I do not know, perhaps you will impose on me that which the Apostle of God was able to do. God chose Muhammad above [all] the worlds and protected him from evils, but I am only a follower, not an innovator (mubtadi'). If I am upright, then follow me; but, if I deviate, straighten me out.
stops.quote_source: The History of al-Tabari, vol. 10 (The Conquest of Arabia), trans. Fred M. Donner, SUNY Press; isnad Ibn Damra from his father from Asim b. Adi, at the dispatch of Usama's expedition two days after Muhammad's death. The popular 'I have been given the authority over you, and I am not the best of you' is a different recension, absent from Tabari.
suggested_refs: The camp of al-Jurf, mustering ground north of Medina for the Syrian expeditions
sources: The History of al-Tabari, vol. 10, trans. Fred M. Donner (archive.org, grepped directly)

stops.name: Medina, the claim to Fadak refused
stops.date_confidence: traditional as to month; the sources date the dispute only to the months after Muhammad's death
stops.campa: Fatima comes to him for her father's estate: the Fadak oasis, the Khaybar share, the properties in Medina. Abu Bakr refuses her, citing a saying of the Prophet that prophets leave nothing to be inherited and that what they leave is charity, and telling her he will not drop anything the Messenger did for fear of going astray. The hadith says she did not speak to him again before her death six months later. Twelver Shia Islam has never accepted the refusal, and the Abbasid al-Ma'mun is said to have reversed it.
stops.quote: Our property will not be inherited, whatever we (i.e. prophets) leave is Sadaqa (to be used for charity).
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr quoting Muhammad, narrated via Aisha; Sahih al-Bukhari 3092 (Book of the One-Fifth of Booty), numbered 3093 in some editions. His second answer in the same hadith: 'I will not leave anything Allah's Apostle used to do, because I am afraid that if I left something from the Prophet's tradition, then I would go astray.'
suggested_refs: The Fadak oasis in the Hejaz, and the long Sunni and Shia literature on its ownership

stops.name: Dhu al-Qassa, the muster on the Najd road
stops.date_confidence: attested, 1 August 632; the site lies east or northeast of Medina toward al-Rabadha and the pin is approximate
stops.campa: The tribes that gave zakat to Muhammad will not give it to Abu Bakr, and half of Arabia writes to Medina offering the prayer without the payment. Umar counsels taking the terms. Abu Bakr refuses in a single sentence about a she-kid, and marches out himself with what troops Medina still has to the muster ground east of the city on the Najd road. Eleven columns are formed there under eleven commanders. Umar will say afterwards that God opened Abu Bakr's chest to the decision and that he came to know it was right.
stops.quote: By Allah! If they withhold from me even a she-kid which they used to pay during Allah's Apostle's lifetime, I will fight with them for it.
stops.quote_source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Zakat, hadith 1399 (numbered 1456 in some editions), narrated by Abu Huraira, trans. M. Muhsin Khan. Umar's later verdict is Sahih al-Bukhari 1457: 'It was nothing but Allah Who opened Abu Bakr's chest towards the decision to fight, and I came to know that his decision was right.'
suggested_refs: The muster ground of Dhu al-Qassa, staging point of the eleven Ridda columns

stops.name: Buzakha, the coalition of Tulayha broken
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month, mid-September 632; the traditional siting near Ha'il is approximate
stops.campa: Khalid ibn al-Walid takes the Asad and the Ghatafan and their allies at Buzakha in north-central Najd, where Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid has been prophesying and drawing the tribes of the centre together. The coalition breaks and Tulayha rides for Syria; years later he will come back a Muslim and fight for this caliphate in Iraq. Uyayna ibn Hisn is sent to Medina in chains and pardoned there. Abu Bakr issues the columns and the pardons from the same room, and does not take the field himself again after the muster.
suggested_refs: The wells of Buzakha in Najd; the rival-prophet movements of Tulayha and of Sajah bint al-Harith

stops.name: Aqraba in Yamama, the Garden of Death
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month, end of Rajab AH 11, December 632; the research pool carried 633 in one lens and 632 in another
stops.campa: Musaylima of the Banu Hanifa holds the richest farmland in Arabia with forty thousand men and a revelation of his own. Khalid meets him on the plain of Aqraba and the fighting is the worst the Muslims have known. The Hanifa fall back into a walled garden, a man is thrown over the wall to open the gate from inside, and the place is remembered afterwards as the Garden of Death. Musaylima is killed in it. Among the Muslim dead are men who carried the whole Quran in their heads and left no copy behind them.
suggested_refs: The plain of Aqraba in al-Yamama, and the walled garden called Hadiqat al-Mawt

stops.name: Medina, the Book gathered off palm ribs and stones
stops.date_confidence: traditional as to month; the sources place the decision in the months after Yamama
stops.campa: Umar comes to Abu Bakr with the count of memorisers killed at Yamama, which the sources give variously as seventy, three hundred and sixty, and five hundred, and says the Book will die with the next battle. Abu Bakr answers that he will not do what the Messenger did not do, and is argued round. He puts it to Zayd ibn Thabit, who says that moving a mountain would be lighter work, and is argued round in his turn. Zayd gathers the text off palm ribs, thin white stones, scraps of leather and the memory of living reciters.
suggested_refs: The first Mus'haf, gathered under Abu Bakr; no leaf of this collection is known to survive

segments.name: The Frontier and the Last Illness

stops.name: Hira, the Lakhmid capital takes terms
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year; the month is inferred from the sequence of Khalid's Iraq campaign
stops.campa: With the peninsula quiet, Abu Bakr turns Khalid north out of Yamama into Sasanian Iraq. Khalid takes Kazima, then Ullays, then Hira, the Lakhmid capital of the Arab Christians on the desert edge of the Euphrates, which pays tribute rather than be stormed; Anbar and Ayn al-Tamr follow. The written order that opens the campaign names a target on the Gulf this army never reaches. Al-Ubulla, the gateway to India, is taken years afterwards, under Umar, by Utba ibn Ghazwan, in the campaign that founds Basra.
stops.quote: Go on toward Iraq until you enter it. Begin with the gateway to India, which is al-Ubullah. Render the people of Persia and those nations under their rule peaceable.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr's written instructions to Khalid ibn al-Walid opening the Iraq campaign, 633; The History of al-Tabari, vol. 11 (The Challenge to the Empires), trans. Khalid Yahya Blankinship, SUNY Press
suggested_refs: Al-Hira on the desert edge of the Euphrates, seat of the Lakhmid kings; the pin follows Wikipedia's 31.98 / 44.39
sources: The History of al-Tabari, vol. 11, trans. Khalid Yahya Blankinship (archive.org, grepped directly)

stops.name: Medina, the letter to two commanders
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year; the month is inferred from the reinforcement sequence in al-Tabari
stops.campa: Khalid and Iyad ibn Ghanm both write for reinforcements, and Abu Bakr sends al-Qa'qa ibn Amr al-Tamimi to the one and Abd ibn Awf al-Himyari to the other, with a letter that draws a line across his own recent war. Men who fought the apostates may serve. Men who were apostates may not, until he says otherwise. The tribes he pardoned in the spring are not to be spent in the summer's conquests. Al-Tabari records that no former apostate campaigned in the conquests afterwards.
stops.quote: Call to arms those who fought against the apostates (ahl al-riddah) and those who have remained steadfast to Islam after the Prophet. Do not let anyone who had apostatized campaign with you until I give my opinion.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr's letter to two commanders, Khalid ibn al-Walid and Iyad, on reinforcing them with al-Qa'qa b. Amr al-Tamimi and Abd b. Awf al-Himyari; The History of al-Tabari, vol. 11, trans. Khalid Yahya Blankinship. Not part of the opening Iraq-campaign letter, though the research pool had joined them.
suggested_refs: The bar on ex-apostates serving in the conquests, and its later relaxation under Umar
sources: The History of al-Tabari, vol. 11, trans. Khalid Yahya Blankinship (archive.org, grepped directly)

stops.name: Ajnadayn, the first pitched battle in Syria
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month, July or August 634
stops.campa: Four columns are loose in Byzantine Syria and Abu Bakr orders them to stop operating separately. They concentrate and meet a Byzantine field army at Ajnadayn in Palestine, and win the first pitched battle of the Syrian conquest. Khalid, recalled out of Iraq across the waterless desert to take command in the west, is the instrument of a strategy whose author is by now in bed with a fever. The news goes down the Hijaz road to Medina and reaches Abu Bakr in the last days of his life. Yarmuk, two years later, belongs to Umar.
suggested_refs: The field of Ajnadayn in Palestine; the Battle of the Yarmuk, often credited to Abu Bakr's concentration order, was fought 15 to 20 August 636, under Umar

stops.name: Medina, the house of Abu Bakr: the testament dictated
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the days before his death; the fever ran roughly a fortnight
stops.campa: The fever holds him about fifteen days. He calls the companions in one at a time and asks them about Umar ibn al-Khattab, and hears the objection that Umar is too hard a man; he answers that the office will soften him. Then he calls his secretary and dictates, so that nobody will have to hold a second Saqifah over his body. He gives instructions too: Ali is to wash him, he is to be buried in his own washed clothes, and what remains of his salary is to go back to the treasury.
stops.quote: In the name of the most merciful God. This is the testament of Abubeker Ebn Abu Kohafa, which he made at that time when he was just going out of this world, and entering into the other; a time in which the infidel shall believe, and the wicked person shall be assured, and the liar shall speak truth; I appoint Omar Ebn Al Khattab my successor over you; therefore hearken to him, and obey him.
stops.quote_source: Simon Ockley, The History of the Saracens, Bohn edition (archive.org, grepped directly). Ockley says only 'his secretary'; Wikipedia's account of the same testament names Uthman ibn Affan as scribe, and the two are not reconciled here. Al-Tabari vol. 11's appointment-of-Umar section is missing from the archive.org OCR.
suggested_refs: The deathbed testament naming Umar, and the objections to his temperament recorded by the companions
sources: Simon Ockley, The History of the Saracens, Bohn ed.

stops.name: Medina, death of the first caliph
stops.date_confidence: attested, 22 Jumada II AH 13; age at death 60, though a devotional variant gives 63 to match Muhammad's lifespan
stops.campa: He dies in his house in Medina on the twenty-third of August, sixty years old, of the fever, having governed two years and about two and a half months, from Yemen to the edge of the Euphrates. He is the only one of the four Rightly Guided caliphs to die in his bed; Umar, Uthman and Ali are all murdered in office. Aishah, in her own journey, is not yet twenty-one and has buried a husband and a father inside twenty-six months, in the same three rooms along the mosque wall.
suggested_refs: The reign is 2 years and 76 days by the calendar, given traditionally as 2 years, 2 months and 14 days

stops.name: Medina, the Sacred Chamber: buried at the Prophet's shoulder
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Umar leads the funeral prayer and they open the floor of Aishah's chamber beside Muhammad's grave. Abu Bakr is laid with his head level with the Prophet's shoulders, which is the tradition's way of saying where it ranks him. Forty-eight hours ago he was governing from Yemen to the Euphrates. Umar ibn al-Khattab takes the office the same day and takes with it the frontier armies, the gathered sheets of the Quran, and the caliphate as something a man can hand on, which nobody knew it was two years ago.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from aishah.journey.json, the Sacred Chamber

stops.name: Medina, the sheets pass to Hafsa and then to Uthman
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the standardisation is dated only to about twenty years after Muhammad's death
stops.campa: The gathered sheets stay in Abu Bakr's keeping until he dies, pass to Umar, and on Umar's murder pass not to the next caliph but to his daughter Hafsa bint Umar, the Prophet's widow, who keeps them in her house. About twenty years after Muhammad's death Uthman sends for them and has Zayd ibn Thabit's commission produce the standard codex, copies of which go out to the garrison cities. No leaf of Abu Bakr's own collection is known to survive anywhere in the world.
suggested_refs: The Uthmanic codex and the garrison-city copies, textual descendants of the Yamama rescue

stops.name: Medina, the pentagon built round three graves
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the source gives only 'eighth century' and no year
stops.campa: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz builds a wall around the three graves, Muhammad's and Abu Bakr's and Umar's, in the century after the conquests, and builds it deliberately as an irregular pentagon so that nobody can walk a circle around it. Circumambulation belongs to the Kaaba and to nothing else. The room that was a bedroom in a mud-brick house is now an enclosure inside a mosque, and its shape is the shape of an argument about what a grave is permitted to become.
suggested_refs: The irregular five-sided enclosure inside al-Masjid an-Nabawi, built to prevent tawaf around the graves

stops.name: Medina, the dome raised, burned, rebuilt, painted green
stops.date_confidence: attested as to years: 678 AH / 1279-1280 for the first dome, 1481 for the fire, 1818 for the present structure, 1837 for the paint
stops.campa: Six centuries on, the Mamluk sultan al-Mansur Qalawun raises a dome of bare wood over the chamber. Qaitbay rebuilds it in brick and lead after the fire of 1481. Mahmud II builds the present structure in 1818 and it is painted green in 1837, which is where the name comes from. In 1805 the forces of Saud bin Abdul-Aziz take Medina and pull down nearly every other tomb dome in the city as idolatry, and leave this one standing. Abu Bakr lies under the most recognisable roofline in Islam.
suggested_refs: The Green Dome of al-Masjid an-Nabawi; the 1805 sparing is reported to have followed Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab's own opposition to its destruction

stops.name: Jannat al-Baqi, the neighbours levelled
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of April the Ikhwan of Ibn Saud level the domes and headstones of Jannat al-Baqi, the cemetery a few hundred metres from the mosque where much of the Prophet's family and most of his companions lie, and leave the ground bare earth. The Green Dome, a short walk away, is untouched a second time. Sunni and Shia communities keep the day as a Day of Sorrow, and every call to rebuild has been refused. Abu Bakr's tomb survives each wave that erases the graves of his neighbours.
suggested_refs: Jannat al-Baqi before 1926, in the photographs taken by Ottoman-era pilgrims
